title: The Quiet Harvest
premise: Tamsin Ravensworth, a pest controller with a talent for rationalizing, is hired to inspect the Hollowmere farmhouse where his family vanished twelve years ago. The house remembers him: mirrors lag a second behind, and a harvest song hums through the walls, one verse short of complete. As Tamsin uncovers that the house feeds on those who sing along, he learns the missing verse was his mother's, sung to keep the family bound and invisible. In the end, Tamsin sings the final verse alone—refusing harmony—and the house, starved of belonging, releases its hold, though he leaves knowing part of himself will always echo there.
about_author: Ada Ravensworth is the pen name of a former rural surveyor who spent years documenting abandoned farmsteads across the English countryside. Their fiction blends folk horror with quiet domestic dread, drawing on the superstitions of farming communities.

chapters.title: The Callout
chapters.summary: Tamsin, POV throughout, takes a pest control job at Hollowmere Farm, telling himself it's coincidence when the address matches his childhood home. He finds no vermin—only scratches at exactly head height on every doorframe. Emotional beat: uneasy denial as old instincts of self-erasure resurface.

chapters.title: One Second Behind
chapters.summary: Tamsin notices the hallway mirror reflects him a beat late; he tests it with a dropped pen and watches the reflection drop nothing. POV stays with him as professional skepticism wars with dread. Emotional beat: the first crack in twelve years of rationalization.

chapters.title: The Client Who Isn't
chapters.summary: Tamsin tries to contact the client who hired him and finds the letter unsigned, postmarked from Hollowmere itself. A neighbor, Mrs. Ellery, warns him the farm 'keeps what it catches.' Emotional beat: isolation deepening—the outside world already treating him as someone who belongs there.

chapters.title: Scratches in the Verse
chapters.summary: Investigating the cellar, Tamsin finds tally marks carved into stone beams, arranged like musical notation. When he hums near them, the walls answer with a fragment of a lullaby he half-remembers. Emotional beat: grief surfacing through melody.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Explanations
chapters.summary: A flashback chapter in Tamsin's memory-POV: the night his parents and sister disappeared, the official story of abandonment, and how he taught himself not to look for explanations. Emotional beat: loyalty to the lie versus the truth he buried.

chapters.title: The House Remembers Me
chapters.summary: Back in the present, doors open before Tamsin touches them, and his name appears in dust on the kitchen table—in his mother's handwriting. He sleeps in his van but dreams inside the house. Emotional beat: the terror of being recognized after years of invisibility.

chapters.title: Mrs. Ellery's Debt
chapters.summary: Mrs. Ellery reveals her own history: her brother sang along with the house in 1974 and became part of the harvest. She gives Tamsin a rule—never finish the song. Emotional beat: reluctant alliance born of shared fear.

chapters.title: The Second Mirror
chapters.summary: Tamsin finds a mirror in the attic showing not the room but the kitchen as it was twelve years ago—his sister Mara setting three places at the table. The reflection looks directly at him. Emotional beat: hope curdling into horror.

chapters.title: What the Fingerprints Belong To
chapters.summary: Following smudged prints up the staircase wall, Tamsin discovers they match his own, aged smaller—a child's hands climbing toward something. The prints stop at the attic hatch. Emotional beat: dawning self-recrimination; he was here before, and left.

chapters.title: The Harvest Log
chapters.summary: In the barn, Tamsin finds a ledger listing names by year, each entry ending mid-sentence. His father's handwriting trails off in 2013. The last page has fresh ink waiting for a new name. Emotional beat: cold clarity about the house's appetite.

chapters.title: Mara's Voice
chapters.summary: The lagging mirror begins showing Mara alive, mouthing words Tamsin can't hear. He starts sleeping in the house to be closer to her, telling himself it's investigation. Emotional beat: longing overriding survival instinct—loyalty weaponized.

chapters.title: The Song Gains a Verse
chapters.summary: Tamsin realizes the house's song has grown longer since his arrival—it's learning from him, harvesting his memories as verses. Mrs. Ellery finds him humming and slaps the tune dead from his lips. Emotional beat: complicity and shame.

chapters.title: Ellery's Warning Fails
chapters.summary: Mrs. Ellery attempts to burn the farmhouse and collapses at the gate, aged decades in moments, whispering that the house took her brother's face as payment. Tamsin drags her home. Emotional beat: the cost of defiance without understanding.

chapters.title: The Attic Hatch Opens
chapters.summary: Alone again, Tamsin opens the attic and finds his childhood bedroom preserved, his old drawings on the wall depicting the house with a mouth. Under the floorboards: his mother's journal. Emotional beat: dread and tenderness intertwined.

chapters.title: His Mother's Journal
chapters.summary: The journal reveals the truth: his mother made a bargain to hide the family from something worse, binding them to the house through the harvest song. The final verse was hers alone—her leash on the thing below. Emotional beat: reframing loyalty as sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Thing Below the Floor
chapters.summary: Descending into the root cellar, Tamsin sees what the house shelters: a vast, patient presence wearing the faces of everyone who ever sang along, including his parents, smiling. It offers him belonging. Emotional beat: temptation at its most intimate.

chapters.title: Refusing the Harmony
chapters.summary: Tamsin nearly joins the chorus—his mouth already shaping the notes—when he hears Mara's voice in the lagging mirror singing off-key, deliberately wrong, keeping herself apart. He stops. Emotional beat: the pivot; love means refusing to blend.

chapters.title: Learning the Last Verse
chapters.summary: From the journal's final pages, Tasmis memorizes his mother's closing verse—not to sing with the house, but over it. The mirrors begin shattering one by one as the house senses his intent. Emotional beat: grim resolve under time pressure.

chapters.title: The Night of the Full Harvest
chapters.summary: On the autumn equinox, the house pulls every door shut and fills the rooms with the chorus of the taken. Tamsin walks through them—his parents' faces pleading—to the kitchen where the song began. Emotional beat: courage sharpened by grief.

chapters.title: Singing Alone
chapters.summary: Climax: Tamsin sings the final verse solo, voice cracking, refusing every harmony the house offers. The chorus falters, the faces unravel, and the presence beneath the floors—starved of belonging—collapses inward as the mirrors all show the present tense. Emotional beat: terrible liberation.

chapters.title: Aftermath at Hollowmere
chapters.summary: Dawn: the house stands ordinary, mirrors merely glass, tally marks faded. Tamsin finds no trace of his family except peace in the ledger—every unfinished sentence now closed. He reports the property clear. Emotional beat: hollow relief, honest mourning.

chapters.title: The Echo That Stays
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Tamsin catches himself humming an unfamiliar verse and stops—but this time he writes it down instead of denying it. Some nights, a mirror lags a half-second, and he lets it. Emotional beat: bittersweet resolution; belonging found in carrying memory rather than erasing it.
